section-59: Polygyny may be sororal (a man marries sisters) or non-sororal. Polyandry may be fraternal or adelphic (brothers share a wife, as historically among the Todas of the Nilgiris and in parts of the Himalayan region) or non-fraternal (the husbands are not related).

Other forms discussed in textbooks include group marriage, in which a group of men marries a group of women, though this is rare and some scholars doubt it ever existed as a stable system. Serial monogamy, common in modern societies, means a person has several spouses in succession through divorce and remarriage.

Rules of mate selection include endogamy (marrying within a group, such as caste endogamy in India), exogamy (marrying outside a group, such as clan or gotra exogamy), hypergamy (a woman marrying into a higher group) and hypogamy (a woman marrying into a lower group). Preferential marriages include cross-cousin marriage, levirate (a widow marries her deceased husband's brother) and sororate (a widower marries his deceased wife's sister).
section-60: Malinowski emphasised the 'principle of legitimacy': every society requires that a child should have a socially recognized father, and marriage is the institution that provides this.

Marriage also performs functions such as establishing a household, creating relationships between two families (alliance), fixing rights over property and inheritance, providing a division of labour, and giving the couple adult status in the community.

Some functions of marriage, such as economic cooperation and education of children, are now shared with other institutions such as the market, school and the state, but marriage continues to be valued for companionship and emotional support.
section-61: Causes of rising divorce in modern society include greater economic independence of women, legal reforms, individualism, changing values about marriage, urbanization, reduced influence of religion and kin, and higher expectations of companionship.

In India, divorce is governed by personal laws such as the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the Special Marriage Act, 1954, and the Indian Divorce Act, 1869 (applicable to Christians). Mizo customary practice traditionally recognized several forms of divorce, and the Mizo Marriage, Divorce and Inheritance of Property Act, 2014, now provides a legal framework for these matters in Mizoram.
Divorce and remarriage create new family forms such as single-parent families and blended families (step-families), which raise new questions about child custody, maintenance and relationships.
section-62: On the basis of authority, families are patriarchal (authority with the father) or matriarchal (authority with the mother). On the basis of residence, they are patrilocal (couple lives with husband's family), matrilocal (couple lives with wife's family) or neolocal (couple sets up a new home). On the basis of descent, families are patrilineal or matrilineal.

On the basis of marriage, families may be monogamous or polygamous. On the basis of size and structure, families may be nuclear, joint or extended. G.P. Murdock described the nuclear family as universal, though later scholars challenged this.

The family of orientation is the family into which a person is born, while the family of procreation is the family a person forms through marriage. Each person usually belongs to both during their life.
section-63: MacIver divided the functions of the family into essential functions (stable satisfaction of sex needs, production and rearing of children, and provision of a home) and non-essential functions (religious, educational, economic, health and recreational functions).

Talcott Parsons argued that in modern industrial society the family has lost many functions to other institutions, but it continues to perform two 'basic and irreducible' functions: the primary socialization of children and the stabilization of adult personalities.

Feminist sociologists point out that the family can also be a site of inequality, unpaid domestic labour for women and sometimes violence, so the functions of the family should be analysed critically.
section-64: The family is a universal institution and the smallest unit of society. It links the individual to the wider society and is the basis of kinship.

It acts as the first school of the child, a source of economic support, a centre of affection and a means of social control. Even when other institutions take over some functions, the family remains the main source of emotional security.
In times of crisis, such as illness, unemployment or old age, the family and kin are often the first and most reliable support, especially in societies with limited state welfare.
section-65: Lewis Henry Morgan, in 'Systems of Consanguinity and Affinity of the Human Family' (1871), distinguished classificatory terms from descriptive terms. A classificatory term covers several relatives under one word (for example, 'uncle' in English includes the father's brother, mother's brother and aunt's husband), while a descriptive term refers to only one relative (such as 'father').
In many Indian languages and in Mizo, kinship terms are more precise than in English and often distinguish elder and younger siblings and relatives on the father's and mother's sides.
Kinship terms are important because they indicate the rights, duties and behaviour expected between relatives. They also show how societies classify and value different relationships.
section-66: Consanguineal relatives include parents, children and siblings, as well as more distant relatives such as cousins. Affinal relatives include the spouse and in-laws, such as the father-in-law, mother-in-law and brother-in-law.
Some societies also recognize fictive kinship, which is based neither on blood nor marriage but treated as kinship, such as adoption, godparenthood or ritual brotherhood.
Anthropologists such as David Schneider argued that kinship is a cultural system of meanings, not simply a reflection of biology, and that different societies define relatedness differently.
section-67: There are two major theoretical approaches. Descent theory, associated with A.R. Radcliffe-Brown and Meyer Fortes, focuses on descent groups such as lineages and clans as the basis of social organization. Alliance theory, associated with Claude Levi-Strauss in 'The Elementary Structures of Kinship' (1949), argues that marriage and the exchange of women between groups are the basis of kinship systems.

Levi-Strauss saw the incest taboo as the foundation of culture, because it forces groups to marry outside and form alliances with others. Louis Dumont applied alliance theory to the study of kinship in South India.
Both approaches are useful: descent explains continuity and membership across generations, while alliance explains the links formed between groups through marriage.
section-68: In traditional families, the husband was generally the head and decision-maker, and roles were clearly separated. Today, especially among educated and working couples, relations are becoming more egalitarian, with joint decision-making and sharing of household tasks.

Young and Willmott described the emergence of the 'symmetrical family' in Britain, in which husband and wife share roles more equally. However, research shows that women often still carry a 'double burden' of paid work and housework.
Changes in marital relations are also influenced by laws on domestic violence, dowry and property rights, and by media representations of marriage.
section-69: Trends in contemporary marriage include a higher age at marriage, more inter-caste, inter-religious and inter-community marriages in urban areas, online matrimonial services, live-in relationships and an increase in divorce and remarriage.
In India, arranged marriage remains common, but many families now combine parental arrangement with the consent and choice of the couple, sometimes called 'semi-arranged' or 'arranged-love' marriage.
In Mizoram, church weddings are the norm, and courtship and individual choice of partner have a long history, though families and churches remain closely involved in the marriage process.
section-70: Studies in India, such as those by I.P. Desai and A.M. Shah, showed that the joint family has not simply disappeared. Many nuclear households continue to maintain 'functional jointness', meaning close cooperation, financial help and regular contact with the wider family.

Factors of change include industrialization, urbanization, migration for work and education, legislation (such as the Hindu Succession Act and its 2005 amendment giving daughters equal coparcenary rights), the changing status of women, and the influence of mass media.

New forms of family, such as single-parent families, dual-career families, childless couples by choice and elderly people living alone, are becoming more visible and raise issues of care for children and the aged.
section-71: Emile Durkheim, in 'The Elementary Forms of Religious Life' (1912), defined religion as 'a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things, that is to say, things set apart and forbidden, beliefs and practices which unite into one single moral community called a Church, all those who adhere to them'.

Durkheim distinguished the sacred (things set apart and treated with reverence) from the profane (ordinary, everyday things). E.B. Tylor gave a minimum definition of religion as 'belief in spiritual beings'.
Elements of religion include beliefs, rituals, symbols, sacred objects, places of worship, religious specialists (priests, pastors) and a moral community of believers.
section-72: Durkheim argued that religion strengthens social solidarity because, in worshipping the sacred, people are in fact worshipping society itself. Malinowski emphasised that religion helps people cope with anxiety and crises such as death.
Karl Marx criticised religion as 'the opium of the people', meaning that it consoles the oppressed but also hides the real causes of their suffering and supports the existing order.

Max Weber, in 'The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism' (1905), argued that certain Protestant beliefs, especially Calvinism, encouraged hard work, saving and rational conduct, which helped the growth of modern capitalism. This shows that religion can also be a source of social change.
section-73: Common classifications include animism (belief in spirits, studied by Tylor), naturism (worship of natural forces, studied by Max Muller), totemism (a special relationship between a group and a plant or animal, studied by Durkheim among Australian aborigines), polytheism (belief in many gods) and monotheism (belief in one God).

Religions can also be classified by organization into church, sect, denomination and cult. Ernst Troeltsch and Max Weber distinguished the church, a large established body, from the sect, a smaller group that often breaks away and demands strong commitment.

Before the arrival of Christianity, the traditional Mizo religion involved belief in a supreme being (Pathian), spirits, and sacrifices performed by priests (sadawt and bawlpu). Today the great majority of Mizo people are Christians.
section-74: Secularization is a related but different concept. It refers to the process by which religion loses influence over social institutions, public life and individual consciousness. Bryan Wilson defined it as the process whereby religious thinking, practice and institutions lose social significance.

Indian secularism is often described as 'sarva dharma sambhava', meaning equal respect for all religions, rather than strict separation of state and religion. The word 'secular' was added to the Preamble of the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, and Articles 25 to 28 guarantee freedom of religion.

Challenges to secularism include communalism, religious fundamentalism, the use of religion in politics and conflicts between religious communities. Sociologists such as T.N. Madan have debated whether Western-style secularism fits Indian society.
section-76: In Mizo society, marriage traditionally involved negotiation between the families, payment of bride price ('man') and a feast. The bride price is shared among the bride's relatives, which shows how marriage connects many kin. Today the church plays an important role in solemnizing the marriage.

Theories of marriage include functionalist views that emphasise its role in reproduction and social stability, and feminist and conflict views that highlight power relations, dowry, domestic violence and the unequal division of labour in marriage.

Problems related to marriage in India include dowry (prohibited by the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961), child marriage (addressed by the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006), and domestic violence (addressed by the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005).

In conclusion, marriage remains a central institution, but its forms and meaning are changing from a duty mainly regulated by family and community towards a partnership based more on personal choice, companionship and equality.
section-77: Characteristics of the family according to MacIver and Page include universality, emotional basis, limited size, formative influence, nuclear position in the social structure, responsibility of members, social regulation, and a permanent and temporary nature (the institution is permanent but each particular family changes).

The joint family in India, as described by Iravati Karve, is a group of people who generally live under one roof, eat food cooked at one hearth, hold property in common, participate in common worship and are related to each other as some type of kindred.

Theories: Murdock argued for the universality of the nuclear family; Parsons emphasised its fit with industrial society; Marxists linked it to the protection of private property (Engels, 'The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State', 1884); and feminists highlighted patriarchy within the family.

In the Mizo context, families have remained patrilineal, but urbanization, education, government employment and migration to cities like Aizawl have encouraged smaller households, while close kin ties and community support continue to be strong.
section-78: Kinship performs several functions: it determines who can marry whom, decides descent and inheritance, assigns rights and duties, provides social security, regulates behaviour through kinship usages, and in tribal societies may also organize political and economic life.

Kinship usages: avoidance (for example, restrictions on contact between a man and his wife's mother in some societies), joking relationship (permitted teasing, for example between a person and the sibling of their spouse), teknonymy (referring to a person through their child's name), avunculate and amitate, and couvade (a custom in which the husband imitates or observes restrictions during his wife's childbirth).

Mizo society is organized into clans and sub-clans traced through the male line, and clan identity has historically been important for social identity and relationships. Patrilineal descent determines the clan name a child inherits.

Kinship remains important even in modern society, particularly at times of marriage, death, festivals and crisis. In India, kin networks also play a role in migration, employment and political support.
section-79: Durkheim's study of totemism among Australian aborigines led him to argue that religion is essentially social: rituals create 'collective effervescence', a feeling of shared excitement and unity that renews social solidarity.

Weber's sociology of religion studied world religions such as Hinduism, Buddhism, Confucianism and Judaism, as well as Protestantism, to show how religious ideas influence economic behaviour. Marx saw religion as a reflection of material conditions and a tool of ideological control.
Religion can be both integrative and divisive. It unites believers, but it can also divide society along religious lines and lead to communal conflict when used for political purposes.

In Mizoram, Christianity, introduced by missionaries beginning with J.H. Lorrain and F.W. Savidge in 1894 and followed by Welsh Presbyterian missionaries, has deeply shaped social life. The church influences education, festivals, music, social norms and community organization. Christmas and New Year are the major festivals, and churches play a key role in social welfare.
section-82: Ogburn and Nimkoff defined social process as 'the ways in which individuals and groups interact and establish relationships'. Social processes are the dynamic aspect of society, while social structure is the static aspect.

The two main categories are associative or conjunctive processes (cooperation, accommodation, assimilation) and dissociative or disjunctive processes (competition, conflict). Some writers also include acculturation, integration and isolation.
Social processes are universal, found in all societies, but their form and intensity differ from one culture to another.
section-83: Continuity in social processes is maintained by customs, traditions, institutions and socialization, which ensure that the same forms of interaction are repeated across generations.

Change in social processes arises from new technology, economic development, migration, education, political movements and contact with other cultures. For example, competition in education and employment has increased with the expansion of formal education and limited job opportunities.
Sociologists see continuity and change not as opposites but as two aspects of the same social reality. Even when new forms emerge, they often combine with older patterns.
section-84: MacIver and Page describe accommodation as the process in which a person 'attains a sense of harmony with his environment'. Ogburn and Nimkoff called it the term used for 'the adjustment of hostile individuals or groups'.

Methods of accommodation include coercion (the stronger party forces the weaker to accept terms), compromise (both parties give up some demands), arbitration and mediation (a third party helps settle the dispute), conciliation (attempts to reconcile parties), toleration (living with differences), conversion (one party adopts the views of the other) and sublimation (redirecting hostile feelings into constructive channels).

Examples include peace accords between governments and insurgent groups, agreements between trade unions and management, and the caste system as a form of accommodation between unequal groups. The Mizo Peace Accord of 1986 between the Government of India and the Mizo National Front is often cited as an example of accommodation that ended a long conflict.
section-85: Robert E. Park and Ernest W. Burgess defined assimilation as 'a process of interpenetration and fusion in which persons and groups acquire the memories, sentiments and attitudes of other persons or groups and, by sharing their experience and history, are incorporated with them in a common cultural life'.

Factors that help assimilation include tolerance, intimate social contact, intermarriage, cultural similarity, equal economic opportunity and shared education. Factors that hinder it include isolation, physical or cultural differences, prejudice, discrimination and a feeling of superiority or inferiority.

Assimilation is a slow, unconscious and two-way process. Critics argue that forced assimilation can destroy minority cultures, so many modern societies prefer pluralism or multiculturalism, which allows groups to keep their identities while living together.
section-86: Green defined cooperation as 'the continuous and common endeavour of two or more persons to perform a task or to reach a goal that is commonly cherished'. Cooperation may be direct (people working together, such as farmers harvesting jointly) or indirect (people doing different tasks for a common end, as in the division of labour).

MacIver and Page also distinguished primary cooperation (in primary groups), secondary cooperation (in secondary groups such as offices) and tertiary cooperation (temporary cooperation between groups for convenience).

In traditional Mizo villages, community work for the village such as clearing paths, building houses and helping in jhum cultivation reflected strong cooperation, supported by the value of tlawmngaihna. The YMA continues similar community service today.
section-87: Gillin and Gillin defined conflict as 'the social process in which individuals or groups seek their ends by directly challenging the antagonist by violence or threat of violence'.

Types of conflict include personal conflict, racial conflict, class conflict, political conflict, international conflict, and communal or ethnic conflict. Conflict can be latent (hidden) or manifest (open).

Karl Marx saw class conflict as the driving force of history. Lewis Coser, in 'The Functions of Social Conflict' (1956), argued that conflict can also have positive functions, such as strengthening group unity, clarifying issues and bringing about necessary reforms. Ralf Dahrendorf linked conflict to the unequal distribution of authority in organizations.
section-88: Biesanz and Biesanz defined competition as 'the striving of two or more persons for the same goal which is limited so that all cannot share it'. Competition is generally impersonal, continuous, universal and governed by rules.
Types of competition include economic (for jobs and markets), cultural, competition for social position and status, racial, and political competition (between parties in elections).

Competition has positive effects such as motivation, efficiency and innovation, but excessive competition can lead to stress, frustration, inequality and conflict. When competition becomes personal and the rules are broken, it may turn into conflict.
section-89: The concept of hegemony was developed by the Italian Marxist thinker Antonio Gramsci (1891-1937) in his 'Prison Notebooks'. He argued that the ruling class maintains power not only through the state's coercive apparatus (police, army) but also through civil society (schools, church, media, family), which spreads ideas that make the existing order appear natural and common sense.

Gramsci argued that challenging hegemony requires 'counter-hegemony', in which subordinate groups develop their own ideas and organisations. He gave an important role to 'organic intellectuals' who emerge from and express the interests of the working class.

The concept is used to study gender (patriarchal hegemony), culture (the dominance of Western media), language and caste. Hegemony is treated as a dissociative process because it involves unequal power, even though it may appear peaceful.
section-90: Elliott and Merrill defined social disorganization as 'the process by which the relationships between members of a group are broken or dissolved'. W.I. Thomas and Florian Znaniecki, in 'The Polish Peasant in Europe and America', described it as a decrease in the influence of existing social rules of behaviour upon individual members of the group.
The concept was developed by the Chicago School of Sociology, which studied crime, delinquency and family breakdown in rapidly growing American cities in the early twentieth century.
Social disorganization is the opposite of social organization. It is always relative, because every society has some degree of disorganization.
section-91: Durkheim linked disorganization with anomie, a state of normlessness during rapid social change. Ogburn explained it through cultural lag, when material culture changes faster than non-material culture.

Other causes include natural disasters, wars, economic depression, unemployment, rapid urbanization, migration, conflict of values between generations, breakdown of family and community controls, and the spread of drugs and alcohol.

In north-eastern India, problems such as substance abuse, HIV/AIDS and unemployment among youth have been studied as examples of social problems that may reflect weakening social controls and rapid change.
section-92: Elliott and Merrill identified three levels of disorganization: personal disorganization (such as crime, alcoholism, suicide and mental illness), family disorganization (such as desertion, divorce and conflict) and community disorganization (such as poverty, unemployment, crime and corruption).

Signs of disorganization include a conflict of mores and institutions, the transfer of functions from one group to another, individualization (people pursuing their own interests without regard to the group), changes in the role and status of individuals, and a lack of consensus on values.
These characteristics appear in different combinations in different societies and must be studied in their specific context.
section-93: Remedies include social planning that anticipates the effects of change, family welfare and counselling services, de-addiction and rehabilitation programmes, youth employment schemes, strengthening community organizations, legal reforms, and value education in schools.

Community-based organizations, churches and NGOs play an important role. In Mizoram, the YMA and churches have been active in anti-drug campaigns and community welfare, showing how civil society can help reduce disorganization.

A balanced approach combines informal social control (family, community, religion) with formal measures (law, police, welfare schemes), while addressing the root causes such as poverty and inequality.
section-95: The classification of social processes into associative and dissociative processes is found in the work of many sociologists, including Ogburn and Nimkoff and Kingsley Davis. Park and Burgess identified four main processes: competition, conflict, accommodation and assimilation.

Park and Burgess suggested a sequence: competition, if it becomes personal and intense, turns into conflict; conflict is resolved through accommodation; and accommodation over a long period may lead to assimilation. This sequence is not always followed in reality but helps to understand how processes are linked.
Different sociological perspectives emphasise different processes: functionalists emphasise cooperation and integration, while conflict theorists emphasise competition, conflict and domination.

Examples from Indian society include cooperation in self-help groups, competition in examinations and elections, conflict between communities, accommodation through peace agreements, and gradual assimilation of migrants into urban culture.
section-96: Kropotkin, in 'Mutual Aid' (1902), argued that cooperation, not just competition, is a major factor in evolution and survival. Cooperation is the most basic and pervasive social process.

Accommodation is a temporary or permanent settlement of conflict without necessarily changing attitudes, while assimilation is a deeper and slower change in attitudes, values and identity. Accommodation can be quick and conscious, whereas assimilation is gradual and largely unconscious.

Examples: cooperation in a Mizo village community clearing a path; accommodation in agreements between rival groups or in peace accords; assimilation in the case of migrants who adopt the language and customs of their new society over generations.
In conclusion, associative processes help integrate society, maintain harmony and allow groups with different interests to live together.
section-97: Differences between competition and conflict: competition is impersonal, continuous, unconscious and governed by rules, while conflict is personal, intermittent, conscious and may break rules. In competition attention is on the goal; in conflict attention is on the opponent.

Marx and Dahrendorf saw conflict as central to social change, while Coser and Simmel noted the functions of conflict in creating group boundaries and solidarity. Gramsci's concept of hegemony explains how dominance can be maintained through consent rather than open conflict.

Dissociative processes are not always harmful. Competition can encourage excellence and conflict can lead to reform. However, uncontrolled conflict can cause violence, destruction and disorganization.
Sociology therefore studies both associative and dissociative processes, since every society contains both cooperation and opposition.
section-98: Elliott and Merrill's 'Social Disorganization' (1934) is a classic work on the subject. Thomas and Znaniecki's study of Polish peasant migrants showed how migration weakened traditional controls and led to family breakdown and delinquency.

Criticism: some sociologists argue that the term 'disorganization' is value-laden, because what appears disorganized may simply be a different form of organization. Later writers preferred concepts such as 'deviance' and 'social problems'.
Social disorganization and social organization are relative; every society has elements of both. Rapid change does not always cause disorganization if institutions adapt quickly.

In conclusion, students should define social disorganization, explain causes (with Durkheim's anomie and Ogburn's cultural lag), describe characteristics and types (personal, family, community), and suggest practical remedies.
section-99: SOC/MD/105 is the Semester II multidisciplinary paper. It is a shorter version of SOC/MJ/103 and focuses on family, marriage and kinship in a simpler form.
Students can use the notes under SOC/MJ/103 for detail, and should give special attention to inheritance, which is added under the Kinship unit of this paper.
section-101: MacIver and Page listed the distinctive characteristics of the family as universality, emotional basis, limited size, formative influence, nuclear position in the social structure, responsibility of members and social regulation.
The family combines biological, economic, emotional and cultural aspects. It is both an institution (a set of norms) and a group (actual members).
Although the family is universal, its form, size and authority patterns vary greatly from society to society.
section-102: Changes in the Indian family include a shift from joint to nuclear households in many areas, greater equality between husband and wife, decline of the authority of elders, increased education and employment of women, and later marriages.

Laws such as the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, and the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, have also influenced family relations.
Despite these changes, the family continues to be important for emotional support and care, and kinship ties continue to be maintained across distance.
section-103: Marriage gives legitimacy to children (Malinowski's principle of legitimacy), creates alliances between families, regulates sexual behaviour and establishes rights over property and inheritance.
It gives the couple adult status and new roles as husband and wife, and later as parents.
Marriage also strengthens social integration by linking families, clans and sometimes villages.
section-104: In India, important changes include the rising age at marriage, legal prohibition of child marriage and dowry, more inter-caste and love marriages in urban areas, and growing acceptance of divorce and widow remarriage.
Online matrimonial sites, migration and education have widened the choice of partners.
In Mizoram, marriage practices have combined traditional customs such as bride price with Christian church weddings, and legal reforms have addressed divorce and inheritance.
section-105: Types of inheritance include patrilineal inheritance (property passes through males), matrilineal inheritance (property passes through females, as among the Khasi, where the youngest daughter traditionally inherits the ancestral house), primogeniture (inheritance by the eldest son) and ultimogeniture (inheritance by the youngest son).

In traditional Mizo society, the youngest son usually inherited the father's house and property and was expected to care for his parents in their old age, an example of ultimogeniture within a patrilineal system.

In India, inheritance among Hindus is governed by the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, amended in 2005 to give daughters equal rights. Christians are generally governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925, while tribal communities may follow customary law.
section-106: For long answers in this multidisciplinary paper, students should prepare the following topics: definition and characteristics of family, types and functions of family, changes in family; definition, forms, importance and changes of marriage; and kinship, kinship terminology, descent and inheritance.

Including examples from Mizo and other North-East Indian societies, such as patrilineal clans, bride price and ultimogeniture, and matrilineal inheritance among the Khasi, makes answers more relevant and earns credit.
